utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The Appeals Chamber is now in session. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. This is case IT-95-10-A, the Prosecutor versus Goran Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Jelisic, you are present in court, and can you hear me? THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Then shall we take the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. I'm Upawansa Yapa, appearing for the Prosecutor, with Mr. Christopher Staker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: For Mr. Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour. My name is Michael Greaves. I am co-counsel on behalf of Goran Jelisic. He is also represented by leading counsel, Mr. Veselin Londrovic. Your Honour, I have one question which I would like to raise before I sit down, and it is this: As Your Honours will know, my leading counsel does not speak either of the official languages of the Tribunal and has been assigned on that basis. He and I do not have a common language. Throughout the proceedings before the Trial Chamber, the learned Judges of the Trial Chamber allowed us to have present, sitting with us at counsel's bench, an interpreter, Mrs. Meliha Zivkovic. Could I ask Your Honours that you extend the same courtesy to us on this occasion and on future occasions when we have to appear before you? Otherwise it makes it very difficult for my leading counsel and I to communicate together about important matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Motion granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm most grateful to Your Honour. May she come into court. She's sitting in the public gallery.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I formally introduce to Your Honours Mrs. Meliha Zivkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You're fully organised now, Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then I would refer to the Scheduling Order recently made, which appointed today as the day on which we would be holding this Status Conference. This Status Conference, as you know, is being held pursuant to Rule 65 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal. The Rule was adopted at the Twenty-First Plenary last November and it came into force on the 7th of December, 1999. The text, in relevant part, reads: "The Appeals Chamber ... shall convene a status conference, within one hundred and twenty days of the filing of a notice of appeal and thereafter within one hundred and twenty days after the last status conference, to allow any person in custody pending appeal the opportunity to raise issues in relation thereto, including the mental and physical condition of that person." So the purposes of this meeting are, broadly speaking, twofold: one, to afford an opportunity to Mr. Jelisic, speaking either directly or through his counsel, to make any representations concerning his appeal, the conditions of detention, et cetera; and secondly, to update him on the situation as regards his appeal. Now, then, Mr. Greaves, would you like to take the floor? Is there anything in particular that you would like to say to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. There's one matter that we would like to raise, which is causing us some difficulties, and it's this: As Your Honours will know, the whole of the trial record was certified as being relevant for the purposes of the appeal by the Registry. We have made a request to the Registry for the copies of the videotapes of the proceedings before the Trial Chamber. The Registry has agreed that we can have those items but has said that it's going to take about six months to produce them. I understand from the Registry that it involves something like 70 individual videotapes of the proceedings. I'm somewhat surprised that it's going to take six months to carry out the copying exercise of 70 videos. One knows only too well that in the commercial world such things are done in an extremely quick amount of time. I appreciate that there are rather more restricted facilities available here, but I'm still somewhat surprised that it's going to take that long. The point is this, and I referred to this earlier on: The transcripts are produced in the two official languages of the Tribunal, English and French. I have access to both of those; I have both sets on both CD-ROM and in hard copy. The transcript is not produced in the languages of the former Yugoslavia, and so the only document or item that my learned leading counsel can use effectively as a transcript is the videotape recording of the proceedings. That's the only access he has in his language to what took place. Of course he's got his notes and of course he's got some assessment from me of what is in a particular passage in the transcript, but it very much hampers his work as leading counsel not to have a transcript. The alternative is to have the tape so that he can go back, following his notes, to use the tapes to assist him in his preparation of matters that are going to be part of the grounds of appeal in this case. What I'm asking Your Honours to do is to encourage the Registry to speed up the process of producing copies of the tapes of the proceedings, and if I could ask Your Honour to use, as it were, your good offices to pass on that encouragement and persuade, perhaps, the Registry to come up with a different time scheme for producing copies of the tapes, then we would be most grateful. If we've got that as soon as possible, then that avoids any risk of further motions for extensions of time that might be consequent upon any delay in receiving those items. [Appeals Chamber confers with legal officer]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Perhaps the Bench better hear from the Prosecution and then from the registrar. Mr. Prosecutor, do you wish to make a contribution?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: It is a short comment that I would like to make, Your Honours. We were not aware of this problem or the request that had been made to the Registrar, and it deals with a technical problem that has been mentioned by the Registrar, about the time that they will take to prepare the tapes. There is one matter which we are -- we do not know what the technical side of it is. There may be instances when some of the witnesses who testify, the protected witnesses, I do not know whether providing the tapes will have a bearing on the position of such witnesses. That is the submission that I wish to make, but, of course, it's a matter entirely in the discretion of Your Honours' court as to the order that Your Honours will make to the Registrar. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. I appreciate that, Mr. Yapa. Now, we will hear from the -- Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I'm not entirely clear what the problem over witnesses is. Both my learned friend and I, and indeed Mrs. Zivkovic, were present throughout the trial. We heard all the witnesses and, indeed, are entitled to hear what they said for the purposes of appeal. So I'm not entirely sure what the problem that my friend is raising is. Is he saying that the Registry shouldn't hear what was said or the technical people shouldn't hear what was said? I think we should be clear on exactly what the problem that is being raised is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Yapa, would you clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My concern was this: We have had previous instances when tapes were made available to Defence counsel, that is, in Celebici, certain tapes were made available. But there was an order made that the tapes not be taken off the Tribunal's premises because of the orders made with respect to protective witnesses. The tapes would be going out of the Tribunal, out of the premises, so that was the concern that I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You mean the chain of custody would have been broken?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: It would be. It would be, Your Honour. It is part of the record of the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is that within your contemplation, Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, if the Registry wants to pay for both my learned friend and I to be here for an extended period of time, sitting in the Defence room watching videotapes, then of course that would be perfectly okay, but it's going to cost an awful lot of money if we have to be here in order to look at the tapes. That's the first point. The second point is that the appellant himself is entitled to have copies of his own trial, and he of course is not going to be allowed sitting in this building, rather than the UN Detention Centre. He, of course, has also heard the same things that we've heard. The second [sic] thing is this: The things which can be found on the tapes can also be found on transcripts, and of course transcripts are frequently taken back to the former Yugoslavia by Defence counsel, and realistically Defence counsel can't be expected to work under those circumstances. I have some knowledge of what happened in the Celebici case because, of course, I was involved in that case as well, and so I followed what has happened in the appeal. I don't know what the rationale behind the decision to order they don't go out of the building was. I understand that tapes were procured in that case for one particular purpose involving an allegation about one of the Trial Judges, and it may be that it was felt right that that, for the time being, should be a matter that was kept within the building. I haven't heard that the reason why the tapes were not allowed out of the building was to do with protected witnesses. But in my respectful submission, it's wholly unrealistic to expect leading counsel to live in The Hague in order to watch videos, to prepare the defence -- the appellant brief. That, I think, is hopelessly unrealistic, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves, this is all under the assumption that the Registry will not be in a position initially to give you a copy of the tapes. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. The letter that was written to us said it would take approximately six months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Six months. Well, perhaps we better hear from the Registry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will try to be as exhaustive as possible on this particular issue. The first thing I would like to say concerning the Celebici videotapes, this was a very special request that was made in a very particular area of the trial, and the access to the videotapes -- it was an edited version of the videotape, it was not what we can see right now on our screens. It was a videotape of pictures taken by camera 3, the camera which only films the Judges, and indeed the request was formulated regarding one particular Judge. The videotapes of this camera number 3 are highly confidential material, which is under no circumstances allowed to leave the Tribunal, which is the reason why these videotapes can only be seen within the premises of the Tribunal. So that closes the issue on the Celebici videotapes. As for other videotapes, we have no problems, as far as communicating trial videotapes are concerned, even if there are some confidential matters raised during the trial. We resort to the code of ethics of the lawyers and we always -- we are always ready to communicate videotapes to the counsel who are part of the trial. But indeed it takes us a lot of time because this request has been formulated not only within this particular case but also for a number of cases and for a great number of accused. So we have envisaged another solution, which would be much quicker, much more efficient, I suppose, and which would maybe calm the fears of the Prosecution as far as protecting protected witnesses is concerned, and that would be to communicate an audiotape, a B/C/S audiotape, to the Defence. It would be much quicker. And I don't know if the Defence agrees to this proposal, but if it does, maybe this would be the ideal solution. [Appeals Chamber confers with legal officer]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Greaves, you have heard what the registrar has had to say. Apparently we need not burden ourselves with the special problems that arose in Celebici. We've heard a reference to camera number 3. I believe with some ingenuity I shall manage to locate it, if I tried, but I am not confident. As for the rest, the registrar has suggested ways and means by which an attempt could be made to expedite the provisioning of the required material to you. Would that be satisfactory to you, if the registrar were to do his best? We certainly would encourage him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I have just a moment, without any discourtesy, to confer with my leading counsel please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Greaves do forgive me for averting my attention away from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Not at all. I was taught that one waited for the Judge, the Judge did not wait for counsel. Your Honour, the position is this: With a reservation which I would like to explain, we would be prepared to accept that proposition which has been made by the Registry. We would want to reserve the right to ask for particular sections of the trial to be made available to us on videotape. I'm sorry. I'm told there's no translation in B/C/S at the moment. It's now present. I'll repeat what I've said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Has it been corrected now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: We would like to reserve the right to make a request to the Registry for particular periods of the trial, which are matters which we need to look at to see what they look like in terms of how the trial was conducted, reserve the right to request specific parts, but obviously limited parts of the trial on videotape as opposed to on audiotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would that present any particular difficulties to you?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at all, Your Honour. But I would like to call everyone's attention on two issues. First of all, these audiotapes are never redacted, so we have to take very specific measures when we deal with audiotapes, so I warn the parties about this. And as for the videotapes, I also ask of the Defence counsel that they be patient when they turn to us to ask for those types of tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves, I take it that you're agreeable to those two reservations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I hope Mr. Dubuisson knows me well enough to know that I'm a reasonably patient individual, and that he can have confidence in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Very good. So I take it that concludes your representations today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That is the only matter that I wanted to raise today. Of course, Your Honour can invite the defendant -- the appellant, I'm sorry, as to whether he has any things he wants to raise. But those are the only things I want to raise today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So I turn to the appellant himself. Mr. Jelisic, you have heard what your counsel has said. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. He wisely wishes to let you have an opportunity to speak directly to the court. Do you have any particular representation to make? THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] I will be very short, Your Honours. There are absolutely no problems in the detention unit. The conditions are very good and the guards are very correct. And as far as I'm concerned, my days are reduced to sorrow, remorse, and a sense of guilt. That is all I have to say. And shame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The Court has listened to you with care and understanding, and what we shall try to do is move the proceedings forward as fast as we could to assist you to compensate for the situation in which you find yourself. What we can do, we shall try to do. You may sit, Mr. Jelisic. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] If possible, I would just like to add one more thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I was under the misapprehension that you had concluded your statement. There is something that you would like to add. Please do. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] I just wanted to add that the administration has provided me with the medical aid. I also am working in the laundry room. So I am very active throughout the day. And I thank you for your concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. You may now sit, Mr. Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That is, I'm assuming you have now concluded whatever it is you wish to say; is that right? THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Yes, that is right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, then, it remains for me just to mark the position at which we have arrived. As I understand it, the briefs of the parties are to be filed by the 15th of May, this year; thereafter, respondent's briefs are to be filed by the 14th of June; and thereafter any briefs in reply are to be filed by the 29th of June. Now, we have heard an allusion to the possibility of certain requests being made, and I'm not in a position, naturally, to say whether those requests will be made, but assuming that no requests are made, we shall be in a position to hear this case in September or shortly thereafter. So that is the position of the Appeals Chamber for the moment. We are in the hands of the parties, but we are ready, willing, and able to go, subject to any requests that you may have on either side, whether by way of extension of time or for some other purpose. Now, perhaps I should add this, just to put it on the record: that as you know, Judge Wang Tieya was an original member of the Appeals Chamber, but he was replaced on 22nd March this year by Judge Pocar, who is on my distant left. So that is the composition of the Chamber as amended on that date, by order of the President of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm sorry to rise again and raise something. I wonder whether it would be possible, really for the assistance of counsel on forward-planning, to identify a provisional date, and I say "provisional," for the next Status Conference that has to be held under Rule 65 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That enables one to plan carefully when one has to be back in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand you to be meaning this: that under the Rule, there is a maximum time period of 120 days, but obviously it could be shorter than that. Is that what you were asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes, and so if we could identify a provisional date, perhaps, that we're working to so that one can plan any other matters that one is looking after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me take counsel with my colleagues and speak with the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: [Appeals Chambers confers with legal officer]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Greaves, that's a very reasonable request. I'm advised that mathematically the outside limit is the 4th of August. What I see on the calendar served up to me by the registrar is that we have, provisionally anyhow, a Plenary meeting slated for the second week of July. I think the last pleading would have been filed on the 29th of June. What that configuration suggests is that we might be holding a Status Conference -- I would like to amend what I said. The Plenary is slated to be in the first week of July; is that right, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's quite right, Your Honour. The first week of July is supposed to see the holding of the Plenary session. So the second week is free, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. So Mr. Greaves, we would make a Scheduling Order fixing the Status Conference for the second week of July. I have spoken of issuing a Scheduling Order, fixing it for some time during that week, for the obvious reason that we are not now in a position to be very definitive about any particular day. You do appreciate, I'm sure, that we have a number of considerations to take into account concerning the disposition of particular members of the Appeals Chamber. But provisionally we are thinking of that week as the week in which this Status Conference should have held.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to Your Honour. That is most helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Well, then, if there are no other matters to be raised, I would now bring the proceedings to an end, merely saying that I think it's perfectly reasonable and I hope that the parties find also that it is a useful purpose in holding meetings of this kind. It is not good enough to allow an appellant to languish in the detention centre without being afforded an opportunity, as it were, to touch base with the Judges in the case. Thank you. Then the court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: adjourned at 4.55 p.m. 22 23 24 25
